summary: Describes the Russian federal standard hash function GOST R 34.11-94, for developers and users who need to compute hashes with it in Internet applications. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5831 describes a hash function from the Russian GOST standards. The function turns a message of any length into a fixed-size 256-bit result through repeated block processing and mixing.

subtitle: An informational description of the Russian GOST R 34.11-94 hash function.

tldr.problem: Developers and users of Russian cryptographic algorithms needed a description of the GOST R 34.11-94 hash calculation for Internet applications.
tldr.mechanism: The function processes a message in 256-bit blocks, applies a step function that uses GOST 28147-89 encryption and a shift-register mixing transformation, then includes the message length and checksum.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5831 is an Informational description and was updated by RFC 6986. It reports the security estimates stated in its own text.

sections.title: Purpose of the Hash Function
sections.content:
RFC 5831 is an informational source about GOST R 34.11-94, a hash function in the Russian GOST family of cryptographic standards. The function maps any finite sequence of binary symbols to a fixed-length 256-bit value.

The RFC explains that a hash can be used with digital signatures so that the signature operation uses the shorter hash value rather than the full message. The document is intended for developers and users who need to calculate this hash.
sections.plainLanguage: A hash reduces a message of any length to a fixed-size value. This RFC explains how to calculate one hash defined by the Russian GOST standard.

sections.title: Inputs and Parameters
sections.content:
The algorithm operates on binary words. The message may have any finite length, while the running hash, checksum, and block values are 256 bits. The initial hash value h0 is a fixed 256-bit word.

The function also depends on substitution tables called S-boxes from GOST 28147-89. That encryption algorithm is used in electronic codebook mode to process 64-bit pieces under 256-bit keys.
sections.plainLanguage: The procedure starts with an initial 256-bit value and uses substitution tables from another GOST algorithm. These settings are part of the hash calculation.

sections.title: The Three Stages of a Hash Step
sections.content:
The step function takes the current hash and one message block, then performs three stages. First, it generates four 256-bit keys from the hash and message block using fixed transformations and constants.

Next, it splits the running hash into four 64-bit pieces and encrypts each piece with one of the generated keys. Finally, it combines the encrypted result with the message block and current hash using a shift-register transformation called PSI. The resulting 256-bit word becomes the next hash state.
sections.plainLanguage: Each step creates four keys, encrypts four parts of the current hash, and mixes those results with the message block. The mixed value becomes the input for the next step.

sections.title: Processing the Whole Message
sections.content:
The calculation keeps a current hash, a running checksum, and the number of message bits already processed. It processes full 256-bit blocks one at a time, updating the hash and checksum for each block.

The final shorter block is padded with zeroes to 256 bits. The algorithm then applies the step function to that final block, the total message length, and the accumulated checksum. The last resulting hash value is the output.
sections.plainLanguage: The message is processed one block at a time. At the end, the algorithm also mixes in the length of the message and a checksum of its blocks.

sections.title: Worked Calculation Examples
sections.content:
The RFC provides test examples that show intermediate values during calculation. It recommends the listed S-boxes and initial value for the examples only. One example uses a message of exactly 256 bits; another uses a 400-bit message split across blocks, with zero padding for the shorter final block.

These values let an implementer compare intermediate calculations, rather than checking only the final result.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show intermediate results so an implementation can be checked step by step. The example settings are identified for testing rather than as universal parameters.

sections.title: Security Estimate in the RFC
sections.content:
The RFC estimates the function's cryptographic resistance at 2^128 step-function computations. It also describes a known method that reduces the estimate to 2^105 operations.

The RFC says that method requires padding the colliding message with 1024 random blocks of 256 bits each, and therefore cannot be used in a practical implementation. These are the estimates and qualification stated by the document.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC gives an estimate of the work needed for attacks and describes one lower estimate. It says that method requires an impractically large padded message.
